person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: method
span.quote: We propose two novel model architectures for computing continuous vector representations of words from very large data sets.

span.label: distributed vector representations of words (word embeddings)
span.quote: The main goal of this paper is to introduce techniques that can be used for learning high-quality word vectors from huge data sets with billions of words, and with millions of words in the vocabulary.

span.label: system-or-tool-building
span.quote: In this section, we propose two new model architectures for learning distributed representations of words that try to minimize computational complexity.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: learn distributed word vectors with a shallow model - CBOW predicts a word from its context, skip-gram predicts the context from the word - so words in similar contexts get similar vectors
span.quote: The CBOW architecture predicts the current word based on the context, and the Skip-gram predicts surrounding words given the current word

span.label: for many languages the available training corpora are only a few billion words or less (a data constraint)
span.quote: the existing corpora for many languages contain only a few billions of words or less

span.label: The exact-match accuracy metric makes 100% unreachable because the models have no morphological information and synonyms count as errors.
span.quote: This also means that reaching 100% accuracy is likely to be impossible, as the current models do not have any input information about word morphology.

span.label: The test set excludes multi-word entities.
span.quote: We have included in our test set only single token words, thus multi-word entities are not present (such as New York).

span.label: Relationship accuracy in the qualitative examples still leaves much room for improvement.
span.quote: As it can be seen, accuracy is quite good, although there is clearly a lot of room for further improvements

span.label: On the Microsoft Sentence Completion Challenge the Skip-gram model alone is worse than LSA similarity; it only wins in combination with RNNLMs.
span.quote: While the Skip-gram model itself does not perform on this task better than LSA similarity, the scores from this model are complementary to scores obtained with RNNLMs, and a weighted combination leads to a new state of the art result 58.9% accuracy (59.2% on the development part of the set and 58.7% on the test part of the set).

span.label: The benchmark's question count is combinatorial: questions are formed by pairing items from short hand-made lists, so the number of questions is far larger than the number of independent facts being tested.
span.quote: The questions in each category were created in two steps: first, a list of similar word pairs was created manually. Then, a large list of questions is formed by connecting two word pairs. For example, we made a list of 68 large American cities and the states they belong to, and formed about 2.5K questions by picking two word pairs at random

span.label: In the semantic half of a semantic benchmark, a correct-meaning answer is scored wrong unless it is the exact expected token.
span.quote: Question is assumed to be correctly answered only if the closest word to the vector computed using the above method is exactly the same as the correct word in the question; synonyms are thus counted as mistakes

span.label: The connection between the benchmark and any practical use is asserted as a belief, not shown.
span.quote: However, we believe that usefulness of the word vectors for certain applications should be positively correlated with this accuracy metric

span.label: semantic - AS FIVE HAND-CHOSEN RELATION TYPES: the semantic half of the test set is five relations (common capital city, all capital cities, currency, city-in-state, Man-Woman), so 'captures semantics' means 'answers analogies of those five kinds'
span.quote: To measure quality of the word vectors, we define a comprehensive test set that contains five types of semantic questions, and nine types of syntactic questions. Two examples from each category are shown in Table 1. Overall, there are 8869 semantic and 10675 syntactic questions

span.label: similarity - AS COSINE DISTANCE AFTER A VECTOR OFFSET, with the three input words removed from the search, so the answer is the nearest remaining word rather than the nearest word
span.quote: Then, we search in the vector space for the word closest to X measured by cosine distance, and use it as the answer to the question (we discard the input question words during this search

span.label: the analogy relation - AS ARITHMETIC ON VECTORS: a relation between two words is the difference of their vectors, and it is applied to a third word by addition
span.quote: we can simply compute vector X = vector(”biggest”) − vector(”big”) + vector(”small”). Then, we search in the vector space for the word closest to X measured by cosine distance, and use it as the answer to the question

span.label: builds-on → neural-network language models
span.quote: techniques based on different types of neural networks

span.label: extends → the two-step NNLM architecture of [13, 14]
span.quote: In this work, we directly extend this architecture, and focus just on the first step where the word vectors are learned using a simple model.

span.label: builds-on → the authors' earlier two-step word-vector training work [13, 14]
span.quote: The new architectures directly follow those proposed in our earlier work [13, 14], where it was found that neural network language model can be successfully trained in two steps: first, continuous word vectors are learned using simple model, and then the N-gram NNLM is trained on top of these distributed representations of words.

span.label: builds-on → the model-complexity comparison framework of [18]
span.quote: Similar to [18], to compare different model architectures we define first the computational complexity of a model as the number of parameters that need to be accessed to fully train the model.

span.label: 1.6 billion — training corpus size; high-quality vectors learned in under a day
span.quote: it takes less than a day to learn high quality word vectors from a 1.6 billion words data set

span.label: < 1 day — training time for high-quality word vectors
span.quote: it takes less than a day to learn high quality word vectors

span.label: The learned vectors capture linear regularities: vector(King) - vector(Man) + vector(Woman) is closest to vector(Queen).
span.quote: vector(”King”) - vector(”Man”) + vector(”Woman”) results in a vector that is closest to the vector representation of the word Queen
